newsitem.title: UK: LME copper carves out fresh high, eyes $2,500.
newsitem.headline: LME copper carves out fresh high, eyes $2,500.

text.p: LME copper prices flew to a one-year peak on Tuesday, bouncing strongly from negative territory and setting the scene for a test of the key $2,500 per tonne mark, traders and analysts said.
Investment funds, commission houses, banks and the trade covering shorts were all said to have contributed to a burst of buying that swept the market higher in the last minutes of the kerb.
"This is an excellent close for copper at fresh highs and it bodes extremely well for tomorrow," said analyst William Adams of broker Rudolf Wolff.

Three month copper touched a peak of $2,495, the strongest since May 20, 1996 when prices hit $2,525. Last official business was at $2,493, up $19 on the day, but in after-hours trading copper was indicated at $2,504/09 at 1655 GMT.
The market came under pressure in the morning after stocks data showed a paltry decline of 475 tonnes on Tuesday after inventories fell last week by nearly 10,000 tonnes.
Nearby lending swamped the market and the cash/threes backwardation contracted by about $25 to $50 while three month prices slid to a low of $2,445.
But after several tests of the downside held, the jitters subsided. By the end of the kerb the cash/threes backwardation had flared back out to $70/$75.
"I think people were convinced they had seen the bottom," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis.
Players may also be anticipating a decision by the U.S. monetary authorities to leave interest rates unchanged, which would be bullish for the metals sector, Bahr said.
A stocks draw on Wednesday of several thousand tonnes would further buoy the market and set the scene for an attack of the $2,500 area.
Most of the other metals followed copper down and back up, but aluminium and nickel remained mired in negative territory.

Aluminium was shaken when stocks rose by 2,050 tonnes, the first increase since early April and prices broke out of a $1,650-$1,680 range they had held for the past 10 days. The market, however, seemed reluctant to sink too deep and stabilised after hitting $1,637 support.
The market ended the kerb with pared losses of $6 at $1,647.
A close below $1,650 is negative, said Bahr.
Stocks also affected nickel, which sunk to a low of $7,650 after inventories rose by 1,260 tonnes. This market also managed a bounce, finishing the day $165 weaker at $7,690.
The other markets mimicked copper, exploring the downside but rebounding back into positive territory.
Zinc edged down to $1,332, but ended the kerb $11 firmer at $1,353, while tin took a look at $5,715 but finished with a $45 gain at $5,790.
Lead added $3 to $623 and alloy finished at $1,500/10, little different than Monday's $1,505/10.
